questions.q: What does text.length count in JavaScript?
questions.explain: A string is stored as UTF-16 code units, and length, indexes and slice all work on them. Most emoji take two code units.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: U+1F372 is above U+FFFF, so it is stored as a surrogate pair: two code units. Spreading iterates by code point, giving one element.

questions.q: The Nigerian flag emoji is two regional indicator symbols. What does this print?
questions.explain: Two code points, each a surrogate pair, so 4 code units and 2 code points. A reader sees one flag, and the segmenter groups both into one grapheme cluster.

questions.q: What is a grapheme cluster?
questions.explain: 👩🏾‍🍳 is four code points (woman, skin tone, zero width joiner, pan) but one grapheme cluster. Intl.Segmenter finds these boundaries.
options: What a reader perceives as one character, which may be several code points joined together
A group of words separated by spaces

questions.q: A sign-up form says "display name: at most 20 characters". Which count should the server check?
questions.explain: The limit is about what people see. A name with a flag or a skin-toned emoji would be rejected unfairly by length, which counts several units per visible character.
options: The number of grapheme clusters, from Intl.Segmenter

questions.q: Which count matters for "the request body may be at most 1 MB"?
questions.explain: Storage and network limits are in bytes. In UTF-8, ₦ takes 3 bytes and many emoji take 4, although each is one grapheme.
options: Bytes after encoding, for example with new TextEncoder().encode(text).length

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: UTF-8 uses 1 byte for ASCII, 3 bytes for code points like U+20A6 (₦), and 4 bytes for code points above U+FFFF.
questions.code:
const encoder = new TextEncoder();
console.log(encoder.encode("N").length, encoder.encode("₦").length, encoder.encode("🍲").length);

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: "Egusi " is 6 code units, so index 7 cuts the emoji's surrogate pair in half. The result contains a lone surrogate, which is not well-formed; JSON.stringify shows it as an escape.

questions.q: What happens when you call encodeURIComponent on a string that ends with a lone surrogate?
questions.explain: A lone surrogate cannot be turned into UTF-8, so encodeURIComponent throws "URI malformed". TextEncoder instead replaces it with U+FFFD. Cutting at grapheme boundaries avoids both.
options: It silently drops the broken half

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: for...of iterates by code point: ₦ and 🍲. split("") splits into code units: ₦ is one, 🍲 is two.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: a is "e" plus a combining accent (5 code units), b uses the precomposed é (4). normalize() defaults to NFC, which composes a into the same 4 code units as b.

questions.q: Where should a shop apply normalize("NFC") to product names?
questions.explain: Normalising at the boundary means the rest of the program can trust stored text. Comparing un-normalised text leads to invisible duplicates and failed searches.
options: Every time two names are compared
Once, when the name enters the system, so every stored name is in the same form and plain === works afterwards
Never; the database does it automatically

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: NFKC applies compatibility mappings: full-width letters become normal letters and the circled digit becomes 2. NFC does not, and the string was already composed, so NFC leaves it unchanged.

questions.q: Why should you usually not store product names in NFKC?
questions.explain: Store what the user meant, in NFC. Build forgiving keys with NFKC or NFKD for searching and matching.
options: NFKC loses information (ligatures, circled or full-width forms become plain characters), so it suits search keys, not the text the user wrote
NFKC is not supported in browsers

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: NFD splits each accented letter into base letter plus a combining mark, \p{M} removes the marks, and lower-casing finishes the key.
questions.code:
const key = (text) => text.normalize("NFD").replace(/\p{M}/gu, "").toLowerCase();
console.log(key("Àkàrà"), key("Àkàrà") === key("akara"));

questions.q: When is stripping accents from text a mistake?
questions.explain: In languages like Yorùbá, tone marks change the word. Removing them is fine for forgiving matching, but wrong wherever values must be exact.
options: In a search box for product names
For usernames, passwords or legal names, where accents can distinguish different values
When grouping near-duplicate products for review

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: ß has no single upper-case letter in the default mapping, so it becomes "SS" and the string grows by one. Case mapping is not always one-to-one.

questions.q: Why should a server use email.toLowerCase() rather than email.toLocaleLowerCase()?
questions.explain: Identifiers need language-neutral rules that give the same result everywhere. Locale-aware casing is for text shown to people in a known language, with the locale passed explicitly.
options: Without an argument, toLocaleLowerCase uses the machine's locale, so the same email can lower-case differently (for example Turkish dotted and dotless i) on different servers
They always return the same result

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Without a comparator, sort compares UTF-16 code units. Capital letters (65-90) come before small ones (97-122), and É (201) comes after all of them.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: An English collator sorts like a reader: case and accents are secondary differences, so É sorts with E, between A and O.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: By default digits compare as characters: "1" before "2" before "5". With numeric: true, each run of digits compares by its value.
options:
Rice 5kg, Rice 10kg, Rice 25kg
Rice 5kg, Rice 10kg, Rice 25kg

Rice 10kg, Rice 25kg, Rice 5kg
Rice 5kg, Rice 10kg, Rice 25kg

Rice 10kg, Rice 25kg, Rice 5kg
Rice 10kg, Rice 25kg, Rice 5kg

Rice 25kg, Rice 10kg, Rice 5kg
Rice 5kg, Rice 10kg, Rice 25kg

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: base ignores both case and accents. accent ignores case but not accents, so "akara" and "àkara" differ.

questions.q: Why does the lesson create one Intl.Collator at module level instead of calling a.localeCompare(b, "en") inside a sort comparator for 50,000 products?
questions.explain: Same comparison, less repeated set-up. A sort makes roughly n log n comparisons, so per-call costs add up.
options: localeCompare gives different results from a collator
A collator loads the locale's rules once; localeCompare with options can redo that work on every one of the many comparisons
Collators sort in place and localeCompare does not

questions.q: A Swedish shop sorts ["öl", "ost", "zebra"]. With new Intl.Collator("sv") the result is ost, zebra, öl. With "de" it is öl, ost, zebra. What should the server do?
questions.explain: In Swedish, ö is a separate letter after z; in German it sorts with o. Neither is wrong. Passing the locale explicitly keeps the server's own settings out of it.
options: Always use "en" so the order is the same for everybody
Use the reader's locale, passed explicitly, because sort order is a language rule
Use the default sort(), which is language-neutral
Use whichever locale the server machine has

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: slice counts negative indexes from the end and returns "" when start is after end. substring treats negatives as 0 (the whole string, length 10) and swaps its arguments, giving characters 2 and 3: "L-".
questions.code:
const sku = "OIL-1L-007";
console.log(sku.slice(-3), sku.substring(-3).length, sku.slice(4, 2) === "", sku.substring(4, 2));

questions.q: A customer's shop name is used in a message. What does this print?
questions.explain: In a replacement string, $& means "the matched text". A replacement function's return value is used literally, which is what you want for data.
options:
Welcome, Deals $& More!
Welcome, Deals $& More!

Welcome, Deals NAME More!
Welcome, Deals $& More!

Welcome, Deals  More!
Welcome, Deals $& More!

Welcome, Deals NAME More!
Welcome, Deals NAME More!

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: padEnd(3) pads to 3 code units. The emoji already uses 2, so only one dash is added, and columns of text with emoji stop lining up.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: There is always one more text piece than there are values. Here the pieces are "", " x " and "", because the template starts and ends with a value.

questions.q: Why is an html tag that escapes every ${value} safer than escaping values by hand?
questions.explain: With hand-written escaping, one forgotten call is a cross-site scripting hole. The tag makes the safe way the only way: literal pieces are yours, values are always escaped.
options: Tags run faster than template literals
The escaping is applied to every inserted value automatically, so forgetting to escape one is impossible
Tags remove all HTML from the result

questions.q: An escaping function replaces < with < first and & with & second. What goes wrong?
questions.explain: Escape & first, then the other characters. Otherwise you escape your own entities.
options: Nothing; the order does not matter
The & of every < just produced is escaped again, so the page shows < as text instead of <
The quotes are no longer escaped

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: English cardinal rules have only "one" and "other"; 0 is "other". For ordinals, 2 is "two" (2nd) but 12 is "other" (12th).

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: ListFormat handles one, two and many items. British English uses no comma before "and"; "en-US" would add one.
questions.code:
const list = new Intl.ListFormat("en-GB", { type: "conjunction" });
console.log(list.format(["rice"]), "|", list.format(["rice", "beans"]), "|", list.format(["rice", "beans", "plantain"]));
options: rice | rice, beans | rice, beans, plantain
rice | rice and beans | rice, beans and plantain
rice | rice and beans | rice, beans, and plantain
and rice | rice and beans | rice, beans and plantain

questions.q: slugify("Àkàrà") and slugify("Akara") both return "akara". Where should uniqueness be enforced?
questions.explain: slugify should be deterministic: same input, same output. Only the storage layer knows which slugs are taken, so it decides how to make them unique.
options: Inside slugify, by adding a random number every time
In the code that saves products, which knows the existing slugs (usually a unique database index plus the product id)
By refusing product names with accents

questions.q: A new seller registers the shop name "Mаma Put" where the second letter is Cyrillic а (U+0430). What does NFKC normalization do about it?
questions.explain: Look-alike ("confusable") characters are not normalization variants. Guard identifiers by restricting allowed characters or checking Unicode's confusables list.
options: It converts it to the Latin a
Nothing; it is a different letter, so the name looks identical to "Mama Put" but compares as different

questions.q: [..."👍🏽"].reverse().join("") no longer shows a brown thumbs-up. Why?
questions.explain: Spread keeps surrogate pairs together, so each code point is valid, but a grapheme made of several code points falls apart. Reverse graphemes from Intl.Segmenter to keep them whole.
options: Spreading splits the emoji into code units and reversing swaps the surrogates
Spreading splits it into two code points, and reversing puts the skin-tone modifier before the thumb, so they no longer join
Emoji cannot be reversed in JavaScript

questions.q: A delivery SMS is 150 characters of plain English and costs one message. Someone adds "₦" to the text. Why can it suddenly cost three messages?
questions.explain: SMS limits depend on the encoding of the whole message. One character outside GSM-7 changes the encoding and the per-part limit, so "length" must be measured the way the channel measures it.
options: ₦ is 3 bytes in UTF-8, so the message is too long
₦ is not in the basic GSM alphabet, so the whole message switches to UCS-2, where one part holds only 70 units
SMS cannot contain currency symbols, so the text is repeated
It cannot; SMS limits are in grapheme clusters

questions.q: A receipt line fits 16 graphemes. Why does truncate keep only 15 graphemes of a long name before adding …?
questions.explain: The limit is about the printed result, so everything that ends up on the line counts, including the ellipsis.
options: The ellipsis is itself one grapheme on the printed line, so 15 + 1 fills the 16 places exactly
To leave room for a line break

questions.q: What does text.toWellFormed() do?
questions.explain: It fixes only broken halves of surrogate pairs. isWellFormed() tells you whether there are any.
options: Replaces every lone surrogate with U+FFFD (�) and leaves everything else unchanged

questions.q: Why count words with Intl.Segmenter (granularity "word", keeping segments where isWordLike is true) rather than text.split(" ").length?
questions.explain: "Great jollof! Thanks" split on spaces gives an empty word for the double space and counts "jollof!" with its punctuation. The segmenter returns real words and marks punctuation and spaces as not word-like.
options: It is the only way to split a string
It ignores punctuation and repeated spaces, and it knows word boundaries in languages that do not separate words with spaces
It counts characters instead of words
split cannot take a space as a separator

questions.q: Write truncate(text, max) that keeps at most max grapheme clusters. If the text is longer, keep max - 1 graphemes and add "…". Use Intl.Segmenter. The program should print the three lines shown in the expected output.
questions.explain: Cutting between graphemes never splits a surrogate pair or a joined emoji, so the result is always valid text of the right visible length.

questions.q: Write counts(text) that returns an object with units (code units), points (code points) and graphemes. The program prints it for "👍🏽 ok".
questions.explain: The thumbs-up and its skin tone are two code points of two code units each; with a space and "ok" that is 7 units and 5 points, but a reader sees 4 characters.

questions.q: Write slugify(text): decompose with NFKD, remove combining marks (/\p{M}/gu), lower-case, turn every run of characters outside a-z0-9 into one hyphen, remove hyphens at both ends, and return "product" if nothing is left.
questions.explain: Decomposing first turns accented letters into plain letters plus marks, so removing the marks keeps the letters. The fallback stops an emoji-only name from producing an empty URL segment.

questions.q: Sort the customer names for an English reader so that case and accents do not push names to the end, and numbers inside names compare by value. Use one Intl.Collator. The program should print the expected line.
questions.explain: A collator sorts like a reader, and numeric: true makes "9" come before "10". toSorted returns a new array and leaves names alone.
questions.expected: Ade, Émeka, obi, Shop 9, Shop 10, zainab

questions.q: Write a tag html that escapes &, <, > and " in every inserted value (not in the literal text). The program should print the expected line.
questions.explain: reduce without a start value begins with the first text piece, then adds each escaped value followed by the next piece. The literal <p class="item"> is left as written.

questions.q: Write cartLabel(n) using Intl.PluralRules("en") so it returns "1 item" or "N items". Do not compare n with 1 yourself.
questions.explain: The rules return a category, and a small table maps categories to words. Supporting another language means another table, not new if statements.

questions.q: Write cleanName(raw) that replaces lone surrogates (toWellFormed), normalises to NFC, collapses every run of whitespace (including tabs and no-break spaces) into one space and trims. The program prints the JSON of the results.
questions.explain: \s in a regular expression matches all Unicode whitespace, including U+00A0. NFC composes "e" and the accent into é, so the length is 4. toWellFormed turns the broken half into U+FFFD.

questions.q: Write wordCount(text) using Intl.Segmenter("en", { granularity: "word" }), counting only segments whose isWordLike is true.
questions.explain: Spaces and punctuation are segments too, but not word-like ones. Numbers such as "2" count as words.
